migrationNotes: Spine: a race clipboard needs sorting before the medal line is drawn, and the same two moves, order then cut, run through ties and a filtered shop table.

Left out of the lesson (still in the course): sql-sort-and-limit-8 (which query returns the three highest amounts) and sql-sort-and-limit-9 (why add id to the sort). Their ideas are taught on the LIMIT and tie screens and are asked again in the skill check.

lesson.title: Make the first row meaningful

lead.text: A table hands back its rows in whatever order suits the database, and nothing promises that the order stays the same from one query to the next. If the order matters, the query has to ask for it. ORDER BY names the column to sort on, and each sort runs one of two ways. ASC puts the smallest value first, and DESC puts the largest first.

So ORDER BY amount DESC puts the biggest orders at the top, and ORDER BY id ASC lists the orders from the lowest id upwards. Without an ORDER BY the words 'first' and 'last' mean nothing, because the rows have no promised order. The picture lists the same six orders both ways.

afterFigure.text: The two results hold exactly the same rows, and only the order differs. It differs because the query asked. ORDER BY is the one part of a query that promises an order, and the way the table is stored or the way the columns are listed promises nothing.

queries.label: Order A
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id ASC;

queries.label: Order B
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id DESC;

lead.text: The same six orders can come back in different orders.

Sorting is the first half of the timekeeper's job. The second half is the line under the third name, and in a query that line is LIMIT. LIMIT 3 keeps the first three rows of the result and drops the rest, so ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 3 means 'put the largest first, then keep three'.

The order of those two steps is built in. The database sorts first and cuts afterwards, which is why a limit on its own finds nothing useful: the first three rows of an unsorted result could be any three. The picture takes the known amounts smallest first and keeps two of them, and then four.

afterFigure.text: A limit is a ceiling and not a target. LIMIT 10 over a result of only two rows returns those two rows, because the query can't add rows that were never there.

queries.label: Two smallest
queries.sql: SELECT amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount ASC LIMIT 2;

queries.label: Four smallest
queries.sql: SELECT amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount ASC LIMIT 4;

lead.text: Put the times in order first, then keep the first rows.

Two orders in the shop are worth 80, so sorting on amount can't decide which of them comes first. Rows that tie can appear in either order, and the database may pick a different one the next time. A limit that cuts through a tie could keep one 80 today and the other tomorrow.

The fix is a second sort column. ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC sorts on amount first and uses id only to settle ties. Every id is different, so no tie survives it. The id is the primary key from the first lesson, which is why it makes such a dependable tie-breaker.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows the tie-breaker at work on the two orders worth 20. Both results hold the same rows, and those two orders swap places. Each result is now fully decided, because the tie-breaker comes last and only matters where the earlier columns tie.

queries.label: Lower id first
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount ASC, id ASC;

queries.label: Higher id first
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount ASC, id DESC;

lead.text: Compare amounts first. When two rows tie, the next sort column decides.

queries.label: Lower id wins ties
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

queries.label: Higher id wins ties
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id DESC;

lead.text: Sorting puts the largest first, and the limit keeps the first rows of that order.
A query can filter, sort and cut at once. The filter always runs first. WHERE chooses the rows that are eligible. ORDER BY then sorts only those rows, and LIMIT keeps the first few of what is left.

So WHERE status = 'paid' ORDER BY amount ASC LIMIT 2 means the two smallest of the paid orders. A pending order is never considered, even a very small one. Reading the query the other way round, as the two smallest orders overall with the paid ones picked out afterwards, would let pending orders use up the places. The picture applies the same pattern to two other questions.

afterFigure.text: Each query in the picture returns one row, chosen from the rows that passed its WHERE. Read a query from the filter to the order to the limit, and its meaning follows.

queries.label: Smallest pending
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending' AND amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount ASC, id ASC LIMIT 1;

queries.label: Largest desk
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE item = 'Desk' ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC LIMIT 1;

lead.text: WHERE chooses the eligible rows first. Then the order and the limit pick from them.

lesson.orientation: Use a deterministic order to decide which rows a limited result retains.
lesson.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: Five runners run a race, and the timekeeper writes their times on a clipboard in the order the runners signed up: 31, 28, 35, 30 and 29 seconds. Medals go to the three fastest.

Nobody can read the medal winners straight off the clipboard, because sign-up order says nothing about speed. The sensible move is to rewrite the times from fastest to slowest and then draw a line under the third. The order of those two moves matters. A line drawn under the third name of the original list would hand medals to the wrong people.

A table is in the same position as the clipboard. Its rows come back in no promised order, so a question such as 'the three largest orders' only makes sense once the rows have been put in an order you chose. This lesson does the sorting and the cutting, and then deals with rows that tie.

intro.promise: By the end you'll order rows so the first one means something, and keep just the top few.

recap.keyIdea: Only ORDER BY promises an order. Add a unique tie-breaker, and LIMIT keeps the first rows of that order.

blocks.text: Back at the race, you sorted first and cut second, as the medal line needs. You kept the first 3 of the ordered times and settled a tie between two 80s by id. The top three known amounts added up to 200.

recap.nextHook: A sorted list can still repeat itself. The bakery's till log that opens the next lesson holds the same few loaves over and over, and the question there is how many different ones were sold.

questions.prompt: A query returns the shop's orders. Which part of it promises that they arrive in increasing order of id?
hints: Ordering must be part of the query.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ORDER BY id ASC explicitly requests increasing ids. Without ORDER BY, the query makes no promise about the order of its result rows.

questions.onCorrect: ORDER BY id ASC. A query promises an order only when it asks for one.

misconceptions.feedback: How rows are stored is not part of what a query promises.
SELECT chooses columns. It does not choose a row order.

questions.prompt: With ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC over known amounts, which id appears first?
hints: Compare amounts before ids.
Which amount is largest, and how many orders share it?
The ties are settled by id in increasing order. Which of the tied ids comes first?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The maximum amount is 80; the lower of its two order ids is 101.

questions.onCorrect: 101. Amounts compare first. The tie between two 80s goes to the lower id.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the winner when the higher id goes first. Check whether id is ASC or DESC.
That amount is not the largest. Compare amounts before ids.

questions.prompt: The known amounts in the orders table are 80, 20, 80, 40 and 20. Sorted largest first, what do the first three rows add up to?
hints: Take the three largest known amounts.
Two orders share the largest amount, so list the amounts from the top, one per row.
Add the first three amounts in that list.
questions.onCorrect: 200. LIMIT 3 keeps the first three rows of the order: 80, 80 and 40.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the two largest amounts only. The limit keeps one more row.
That takes four rows. The limit stops after the third.

questions.prompt: A query reads WHERE status = 'paid' ORDER BY amount ASC, id ASC LIMIT 2. Which set of orders does it return?
hints: Read the filter, direction and limit together.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: WHERE first keeps paid rows, ORDER BY amount ASC puts the smallest amounts first, and LIMIT 2 keeps the first two. id provides a stable order for ties.

choices.label: The first two rows stored on disk

questions.onCorrect: The two smallest paid orders. WHERE chooses the rows, then ASC and LIMIT 2 pick from them.

misconceptions.feedback: ASC runs from the smallest upwards, so this takes the other end.
WHERE and ORDER BY decide the rows, not how they are stored.

questions.prompt: How many rows can LIMIT 10 return when only four rows satisfy WHERE?
hints: LIMIT is an upper bound.
There are only four eligible rows.
Use the smaller of the eligible-row count and the limit; LIMIT adds no rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A limit does not create records; the result contains the four eligible rows.

questions.onCorrect: 4. LIMIT is a ceiling. It never adds rows that are not there.

misconceptions.feedback: LIMIT sets a ceiling, not a target. It cannot invent rows.

questions.prompt: Two rows tie on amount. How do you make their order deterministic?
hints: A unique secondary sort key separates the tied rows.

acceptedIdeas: Add a unique id as a tie-breaker
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Add a unique id after amount in ORDER BY. It settles ties on amount so the same rows have a defined order.

choices.label: Add a unique id as a tie-breaker

questions.onCorrect: Add a unique id as a tie-breaker. A second sort column makes the order fully decided.

misconceptions.feedback: Without ORDER BY nothing about the order is promised.
LIMIT cuts a result. It does not sort one.

questions.prompt: Five runners finish a race in 31, 28, 35, 30 and 29 seconds. The three fastest win medals. What is the slowest time that still wins a medal?
hints: Which order puts the medal winners first?
Medals go to the first three in that order.
Find the third time when they are listed fastest first.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: In order the times are 28, 29, 30, 31 and 35. The first three win, and the third is 30.

questions.onCorrect: 30. You put the times in order first and then kept the first three. ORDER BY and LIMIT do exactly that.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the slowest runner overall. Medals go to the fastest three.

questions.prompt: Which query returns the three highest amounts?
hints: Which direction puts the highest amount first?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: DESC puts the highest amounts first, and LIMIT 3 keeps the first three of them.

questions.onCorrect: Order the rows so the highest come first, then LIMIT keeps the first rows of that order.

misconceptions.feedback: ASC starts at the smallest amount, so this keeps the lowest rows.
With no ORDER BY the rows have no promised order, so the first rows could be any.

questions.prompt: Why add id to the sort?
hints: What decides the order of two rows with the same amount?

acceptedIdeas: Without it, the order of tied rows is not promised.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Rows that tie on amount need a second sort column, or their order is left open.

questions.onCorrect: A second sort column settles ties. Without it the order of tied rows is not promised.

choices.label: Without it, the order of tied rows is not promised.
Because id makes the amounts larger.
Because LIMIT needs a second column.

misconceptions.feedback: The id never changes an amount. It only separates rows that tie.
LIMIT works with any ordering. The extra column is about ties.

questions.prompt: Four orders have amounts 50, 70, 70 and 90. What is the sum of the amounts returned by ORDER BY amount ASC LIMIT 2?
hints: Which direction does ASC use?
List the amounts from smallest upward.
Add the first two in that list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ascending gives 50, 70, 70, 90. The first two are 50 and 70, and they add up to 120.

questions.onCorrect: 120. ASC puts the smallest first, and LIMIT 2 keeps the first two.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two largest. ASC starts at the smallest amount.
